title: Epilogue, Chapter 2
paragraphs: He was ill for a long time. But it was not the horrors of prison life, the hard labor, the bad food, the shaved head, or the patched clothes that crushed him. What did he care about all those trials and hardships? He was even glad of the hard work -- physically exhausted, he could at least count on a few hours of peaceful sleep. And what was the food to him -- the watery cabbage soup with beetles floating in it? As a student, he had often gone without even that. His clothes were warm and suited to his way of life. He didn't even feel the fetters. Was he ashamed of his shaved head and striped convict's coat? Before whom? Before Sonia? Sonia was afraid of him -- how could he be ashamed before her? And yet he was ashamed, even before Sonia, and he tormented her for it with his contemptuous, rough manner. But it wasn't his shaved head or his chains that shamed him. His pride had been wounded to the core. It was wounded pride that made him ill. Oh, how happy he would have been if he could have blamed himself! He could have borne anything then, even shame and disgrace. But he judged himself harshly, and his embittered conscience found no particularly terrible fault in his past -- only a simple blunder that could happen to anyone. What shamed him was that he, Raskolnikov, had so hopelessly, so stupidly destroyed himself through some blind decree of fate, and now had to submit and accept the "idiocy" of a court's verdict if he was ever to have any peace.

A vague, pointless anxiety in the present, and in the future a ceaseless sacrifice leading to nothing -- that was all that lay before him. And what comfort was it that at the end of eight years he would be only thirty-two and able to start a new life? What was there to live for? What to look forward to? Why should he strive? To live in order to exist? But he had been ready a thousand times before to give up existence for the sake of an idea, a hope, even a fantasy. Mere existence had always been too little for him; he had always wanted more. Perhaps it was precisely the strength of his desires that had made him think he was a man to whom more was permitted than to others.

If only fate had sent him repentance -- burning repentance that would have torn his heart and robbed him of sleep, the kind of repentance whose terrible agony brings visions of the noose or the river! Oh, he would have welcomed it! Tears and torment would at least have been life. But he did not repent of his crime.

At least he might have found relief in raging at his own stupidity, as he had raged at the grotesque blunders that had landed him in prison. But now, in prison, in this new freedom from distraction, he thought over and reexamined all his actions again, and by no means found them as blundering and grotesque as they had seemed at the fatal time.

"In what way," he asked himself, "was my theory stupider than the others that have swarmed and clashed since the beginning of the world? One only has to look at the thing independently, broadly, free from the influence of commonplace ideas, and my theory will by no means seem so... strange. Oh, you skeptics and penny philosophers -- why do you always stop halfway!"

"Why does my act strike them as so horrible?" he said to himself. "Because it was a crime? What does 'crime' mean? My conscience is clear. Yes, it was a legal crime -- the letter of the law was broken and blood was shed. Fine -- punish me for breaking the letter of the law, and leave it at that. Of course, in that case, many of humanity's benefactors who seized power instead of inheriting it should have been punished at their very first step. But those men succeeded, and so they were right -- and I failed, and so I had no right to take that step."
It was only in that -- only in the fact that he had failed and then confessed -- that he recognized his crime.

He also suffered from another question: why hadn't he killed himself? Why had he stood staring at the river and chosen confession instead? Was the will to live really so strong? Was it so hard to overcome? Hadn't Svidrigailov overcome it, even though he feared death?

In his misery, he asked himself this question and could not understand that at the very moment he had stood gazing into the river, he had perhaps already sensed the fundamental falseness in himself and in his convictions. He did not understand that this dim awareness might be the promise of a future crisis, of a new way of seeing life, of his eventual resurrection.

He preferred to attribute it to the dead weight of instinct, which he couldn't overcome -- yet more weakness, more cowardice. He looked at his fellow prisoners and was amazed at how much they all loved life, how much they valued it. It seemed to him they loved and treasured life more in prison than they had in freedom. What terrible agonies and deprivations some of them -- the vagrants, for instance -- had endured! Could they really care so much about a ray of sunshine, a patch of primeval forest, a cold spring hidden away in some remote spot, which a tramp had marked three years ago and longed to see again the way he might long for a sweetheart, dreaming of the green grass around it and the bird singing in the bush? As he looked further, he found even more inexplicable examples.

In prison, of course, there was much he did not see and did not want to see. He lived with his eyes cast down, so to speak. The sight of those around him was repellent and unbearable. But gradually, things began to surprise him, and he started, almost against his will, to notice what he had never suspected before. What surprised him most was the terrible, impassable gulf between himself and everyone else. They seemed to be a different species. He looked at them and they at him with suspicion and hostility. He understood the reasons for his isolation, but he had never imagined until now how deep and strong those reasons were. There were some Polish exiles, political prisoners, among them, who simply looked down on the rest as ignorant peasants. But Raskolnikov couldn't see it that way. He noticed that these "ignorant" men were in many ways far wiser than the Poles. There were also some Russians who were just as contemptuous -- a former officer and two seminary students. Raskolnikov saw their mistake as clearly as anything. He was disliked and avoided by everyone; eventually they began to hate him -- and he couldn't understand why. Men who had been far more guilty despised and laughed at his crime.
"You're a gentleman," they would say. "You shouldn't be hacking people up with an axe. That's not a gentleman's work."

In the second week of Lent, it was his turn to take communion with his group. He went to church and prayed with the others. One day a fight broke out -- he never knew how it started. They all turned on him at once in a fury.
"You're a godless man! You don't believe in God!" they shouted. "You ought to be killed!"

He had never spoken to them about God or his beliefs, but they wanted to kill him as an infidel. He said nothing. One prisoner rushed at him in a blind frenzy. Raskolnikov stood his ground calmly and silently; not a brow twitched, not a muscle of his face moved. The guard managed to get between them just in time, or there would have been bloodshed.

There was another question he couldn't resolve: why did they all love Sonia so much? She didn't try to win their favor and rarely met them, coming only sometimes to visit him at work for a few minutes. Yet everyone knew her. They knew she had followed him here, knew how and where she lived. She never gave them money or did them any particular favors. Only once, at Christmas, she sent them all gifts of pies and rolls. But gradually a closer bond developed between them and Sonia. She wrote letters for them and mailed them to their families. When relatives of the prisoners visited the town, they left presents and money with Sonia at the prisoners' request. Their wives and sweethearts knew her and went to see her. And when she visited Raskolnikov at work, or met a group of prisoners on the road, they all removed their hats. "Dear little mother Sofya Semyonovna -- you are our kind, gentle little mother," these coarse, branded criminals would say to that frail young woman. She would smile and bow to them, and everyone was delighted when she smiled. They admired even the way she walked, and would turn to watch her go. They admired her for being so small, and couldn't decide what they admired most about her. They even came to her when they were ill.

He was in the hospital from the middle of Lent until after Easter. When he recovered, he recalled the dreams he had had during his fever and delirium. He had dreamt that the entire world was doomed by a terrible new plague that had come to Europe from the depths of Asia. Everyone was to perish except a very few chosen ones. Some new kind of microbes had appeared, attacking human bodies, but these microbes were endowed with intelligence and will. People infected by them instantly went mad and violent. But never had people considered themselves so wise, so unshakably in possession of the truth, as these infected victims. Never had they been more confident in their judgments, their scientific conclusions, their moral convictions. Entire villages, entire cities and nations went mad from the infection. Everyone was agitated and no one understood anyone else. Each person believed that he alone possessed the truth, and suffered looking at the others, beating his breast, weeping, wringing his hands. They could not agree on what was evil and what was good, could not decide whom to blame and whom to acquit. They killed one another in a kind of senseless rage. They gathered in armies to march against each other, but even on the march the armies would splinter, the soldiers turning on one another, stabbing, slashing, biting, and devouring each other. Alarm bells rang all day in the cities; people rushed together, but no one knew why they had been summoned or who was summoning them. The most ordinary trades were abandoned, because everyone had his own ideas, his own improvements, and they couldn't agree. The fields were abandoned too. People would meet in groups, agree on something, swear to work together -- then immediately start doing something completely different from what they had planned. They accused one another, fought, and killed. There were fires and famine. Everything and everyone was caught up in destruction. The plague spread further and further. Only a handful of people in the entire world could be saved. They were a pure, chosen people, destined to found a new race and a new life, to renew and purify the earth. But no one had seen these people, no one had heard their words or their voices.

It troubled Raskolnikov that this senseless dream clung to his memory so painfully, that the impression of his feverish delirium lasted so long. The second week after Easter arrived. Warm, bright spring days had come. In the prison ward, the barred windows beneath which the sentinel paced were opened. Sonia had been able to visit him only twice during his illness -- each time she had to get permission, and it was difficult. But she often came to the hospital courtyard, especially in the evening, sometimes just to stand for a moment and look up at the windows of the ward.

One evening, when he was nearly recovered, Raskolnikov fell asleep. Waking, he happened to go to the window, and at once saw Sonia in the distance at the hospital gate. She seemed to be waiting for someone. Something pierced his heart at that instant. He shuddered and stepped away from the window. The next day Sonia didn't come, nor the day after. He noticed that he was waiting for her with growing anxiety. Finally he was discharged. Returning to the prison, he learned from the other convicts that Sofya Semyonovna was ill and confined to her bed.

He was deeply worried and sent someone to ask about her. He soon learned that her illness was not dangerous. When she heard he was anxious about her, Sonia sent him a note written in pencil, telling him she was much better, that she had a slight cold, and that she would soon, very soon come to see him at work. As he read it, his heart ached.

It was another warm, bright day. Early in the morning, around six, he went to work on the riverbank where they ground alabaster, near a kiln in a shed. Only three prisoners had been sent. One went with the guard to the fortress for a tool; the other began preparing firewood and loading the kiln. Raskolnikov came out of the shed onto the riverbank, sat down on a pile of logs, and began gazing at the wide, deserted river. From the high bank, a vast landscape spread before him. From the far bank, the faint sound of singing drifted across the water. Out in the boundless steppe, drenched in sunlight, he could just make out the nomads' tents, like tiny dark specks. There was freedom out there, there lived other people utterly unlike those here; there, time itself seemed to stand still, as if the age of Abraham and his flocks had never passed. Raskolnikov sat gazing, and his thoughts dissolved into daydreams, into pure contemplation. He thought of nothing in particular, but a vague restlessness stirred and troubled him. Suddenly he found Sonia beside him. She had approached soundlessly and sat down next to him. It was still very early; the morning air was still sharp. She wore her old, worn burnous and the green shawl. Her face still showed signs of illness -- it was thinner and paler. She gave him a joyful, welcoming smile, but held out her hand with her usual timidity. She was always timid about offering him her hand, and sometimes didn't offer it at all, as though afraid he would push it away. He always took her hand as though with reluctance, always seemed annoyed to see her, and sometimes sat in stubborn silence throughout her entire visit. There were times she trembled before him and went away in deep grief. But this time their hands did not part. He stole a quick glance at her and looked down at the ground without speaking. They were alone. No one had seen them. The guard had turned away for the moment.

How it happened he could not say. But all at once something seemed to seize him and hurl him at her feet. He wept and threw his arms around her knees. For the first moment she was terrified -- her face went white. She leapt up and looked at him, trembling. But in that same instant she understood, and a light of infinite happiness shone in her eyes. She knew -- she had no doubt -- that he loved her, loved her beyond everything, and that at last the moment had come.

They tried to speak but could not. Tears stood in their eyes. They were both pale and thin; but in those sick, pale faces shone the dawn of a new future, a full resurrection into new life. Love had renewed them; the heart of each held infinite wellsprings of life for the heart of the other.

They resolved to wait and be patient. They still had seven years ahead of them, and what terrible suffering and what boundless happiness lay before them! But he had risen again, and he knew it, felt it with every fiber of his being. And she -- she lived only in his life.

That evening, after the barracks were locked, Raskolnikov lay on his plank bed and thought about her. He had even noticed that day that all the prisoners who had been his enemies seemed to look at him differently. He had even spoken to them, and they had answered in a friendly way. He remembered this now and thought it could not be otherwise. Wasn't everything bound to change now?

He thought of her. He remembered how he had constantly tormented her and wounded her heart. He recalled her pale, thin little face. But these memories scarcely troubled him now; he knew with what infinite love he would repay all her suffering. And what were all, all the agonies of the past! Everything -- even his crime, his sentence, his imprisonment -- seemed to him now, in the first rush of feeling, like some external, alien fact that had nothing to do with him. But he could not think coherently about anything that evening and could not have analyzed anything consciously. He was simply feeling. Life had taken the place of theory, and something entirely different would now work itself out in his mind.

Under his pillow lay the New Testament. He picked it up mechanically. It was Sonia's -- the same book from which she had read him the raising of Lazarus. At first he had been afraid she would pester him about religion, talk about the gospels, and force books on him. But to his great surprise she had never once brought it up and had not even offered him the Testament. He had asked her for it himself, not long before his illness, and she had brought the book without a word. He had not opened it until now.
He did not open it now either, but a thought passed through his mind: "Can her beliefs become mine? Her feelings, her aspirations, at least..."

She too had been deeply shaken that day, and during the night she fell ill again. But she was so happy -- so unexpectedly happy -- that she was almost afraid of her own happiness. Seven years -- only seven years! At the start of their happiness, in certain moments, they were both ready to look at those seven years as though they were seven days. He did not know that this new life would not come to him for nothing, that he would have to pay dearly for it, that it would cost him great effort, great suffering.

But that is the beginning of a new story -- the story of a man's gradual renewal, his gradual regeneration, his passage from one world into another, his initiation into a new and unknown life. That might be the subject of a new tale, but our present story is ended.
